history.body: From a small group of Japanese immigrant families in 1925 to a vibrant community today. We honor our heritage while building connections for the future.
history.missionText: To preserve and share our Japanese heritage and its traditions with the community through cultural, educational, and social activities.
history.videoTitle: A video tour of the Southeast Japanese School & Community Center
history.videoCaption: A look inside the center, its history, and its traditions.

milestones.text: Reverend Tsunesuke Hayashi had been teaching Japanese at the Friends Japanese Church since 1923. In 1925 the community broke ground on a school of its own on the Nawa Ranch, beside the land the center stands on today, and he became its first principal.
milestones.photoAlt: The Nawa Ranch outside Norwalk, where the first Japanese language school was built in 1925

milestones.text: Parents and community members paid for a new school building, raised under Takuichi Nakatani on the site the center still occupies. Judo classes began in 1931, kendo in 1934.
milestones.photoAlt: The community gathered outside the new Norwalk Gakuen school building at its 1930 dedication

milestones.text: The Gakuen had become the heart of Japanese immigrant life in Norwalk — Saturday classes for the children, and the community's own gatherings the rest of the year. Enrollment reached 250 before the war.
milestones.photoAlt: Members of the Gakuen Agriculture Union gathered for a banquet in 1936

milestones.text: Every Japanese American family in Norwalk was incarcerated, and the school building was rented to an American church. Families returned to the area in 1946, and Norwalk Gakuen reopened on June 22, 1957 under Principal Shuyu Kurai.
milestones.photoAlt: Two archival photographs from the war years — the flag over the Manzanar incarceration camp, and a judoka seated in seiza

milestones.text: On April 11 the school was granted nonprofit status and took the name it carries today. The Youth Activities Group — now Norwalk Youth Sports — was established the same year, parents hosted the first Summer Festival in 1963, and a kendo class formed in 1964.
milestones.photoAlt: The kendo class in 1965, in bogu, with their instructors

milestones.text: Years of fundraising opened a new building with a gymnasium, kitchen and three classrooms. Bonsai, ballroom dance and tea ceremony classes followed, and Hikari Taiko formed in 1978.
milestones.photoAlt: The hall full of guests at the 1977 new building dedication, hung with koinobori

milestones.text: After four years of fundraising, an annex was dedicated in July with ten more classrooms, a multipurpose room and two bathrooms.
milestones.photoAlt: Members gathered for the 1994 groundbreaking outside the new annex

milestones.text: The center celebrated its 100th anniversary on July 26, with 132 students enrolled at the Gakuen and four generations together in the hall.
milestones.photoAlt: Visitors looking through the group history displays at the 100th anniversary celebration

classes.caption: Class Descriptions
classes.lede: The school includes a kindergarten program for children who are five years old. The regular program is recommended for children six years and older, and adult classes meet online.

levels.name: Kindergarten Program
levels.description: Children who are five years old learn the Japanese culture through organized activities involving crafts, songs, and the Japanese language.
points: Crafts, songs, and the Japanese language

levels.name: Beginning Level Japanese
levels.description: Children will be introduced to the language with emphasis on listening and speaking, with some reading and writing. Culture lessons and crafts will be integrated into the lessons.

levels.name: Elementary Level
levels.description: Students will continue to develop basic conversational skills as well as reading and writing of short sentences. Students will be able to hold short conversations on topics relating to daily life. Culturally appropriate behavior as well as annual cultural festivities will be integrated into the lesson.
levels.photoAlt: Elementary level students with their teacher

levels.name: Intermediate Level Japanese
levels.description: Students will further develop their abilities to function in a Japanese speaking environment through listening, speaking, reading, and writing. Students learn how to request information, converse in a participatory manner, and exchange detailed factual information. Classes will be conducted in Japanese for a majority of the time, including participation in discussions and activities in Japanese.
points: Conducted in Japanese most of the time
levels.photoAlt: Intermediate level students with their teacher

levels.name: Advanced Level Japanese
levels.description: Students will continue refining their ability to listen, speak, read, and write in Japanese. Students will be able to converse and discuss topics of current interest and express personal opinions. They will be able to narrate, describe, and explain. Students will be able to initiate, sustain, and close a general conversation with a number of communicative strategies. Students will use Japanese in culturally authentic and practical situations, incorporating idiomatic expressions, and will learn the appropriate language to use in a variety of social interactions.
points: Topics of current interest and personal opinions
levels.photoAlt: Advanced level students from levels 9 through 12

levels.name: Adult Classes
levels.description: Beginning Level students will learn basic Japanese which will enable the student to function as a tourist in Japan. The classes are held 70 minutes every Saturday, and students are welcome to join more than one class each week for additional review. Reading and writing of the script will be incorporated into the lessons, with emphasis on the spoken language. The classes will be on a continuing basis up to the advanced level, in which idiomatic phrases and appropriate language for a variety of social interactions will be taught. Adult classes are online this year with 3 levels.
levels.photoAlt: Adult students in an online Japanese class

levels.name: After School Shuji Class
levels.description: Students may participate in after school Shuji class, or brush calligraphy. Students learn this art form using the traditional brush and ink. No prior experience is necessary. Shuji helps students to learn proper lettering techniques. It also instills good mental attitude and enthusiasm toward studies, as well as training for perseverance. Shuji class begins after lunch from 12:30 – 1:30 PM. Students must purchase their own equipment (approximately $30).
levels.photoAlt: Students and teachers in the after-school shuji calligraphy class

year.caption: Annual Cultural Events
year.lede: Our program provides a rich variety of cultural activities, including monthly cultural events to enhance cultural experience and understanding.

months.title: Oshogatsu
months.description: In January, to welcome the new year, the students are served ozoni.
months.photoAlt: Students eating ozoni to welcome the new year

months.title: Setsubun
months.description: In the beginning of February, students celebrate Setsubun. They are given roasted soybeans to eat to ensure their good luck throughout the new year.
months.photoAlt: Students wearing oni masks they made for Setsubun

months.title: Hinamatsuri
months.description: March is Hinamatsuri — a doll festival to celebrate girls. Boys and girls alike observe the hina-ningyo display that showcases the Emperor and Empress's court.
months.photoAlt: Students seated in front of the hina-ningyo doll display

months.title: Hanami
months.description: Students learn about Japan's appreciation for nature and celebrate the arrival of spring.

months.title: Ohanashikai · Kodomo no Hi
months.description: Students showcase what they have learned in the past year through a speech program held onstage. On Children's Day, the koi no bori — fish flags — and samurai helmets and dolls are displayed, and children learn about this festival through a presentation.
months.photoAlt: Students beneath koinobori carp streamers and a samurai doll display

months.when: Cultural Festival · second weekend in June
months.title: Tanabata
months.description: The star festival is celebrated by allowing the students to write down their wishes and hang them on a traditional tanabata tree. Our school holds an annual Cultural Festival the second weekend in June. School ends at the end of June, with vacation time during the month of July.
months.photoAlt: Students beside a tanabata bamboo hung with their paper wishes

months.title: School Begins
months.description: School begins on the third Saturday of the month.
months.photoAlt: The Gakuen teaching staff at the start of the school year

months.title: Back to School
months.description: Back to School Day is held to learn about our curriculum and school program.
months.photoAlt: Students seated on the floor watching a koto demonstration

months.title: Undokai
months.description: Undokai is an annual athletic event held in October. Every student attending the Southeast Japanese School will participate in the various sport games at a nearby park.
months.photoAlt: Students playing a team game at the undokai

months.title: Shichi-go san
months.description: The Seven-five-three Festival is held in November each year at local shrines in Japan. At Southeast Japanese School, students learn about the festival, and a few students will have the opportunity to dress in the traditional kimono for the occasion.

months.title: New Years
months.description: Students experience a sample of the oshogatsu festivities by viewing traditional mochi pounding and tasting toshikoshi soba.

history.caption: History of the School
body: Southeast Japanese Language School (Southeast Gakuen) was first established in 1925 as Norwalk Gakuen to teach Japanese to children of Japanese immigrants. In 1962, the school was renamed Southeast Japanese School. Presently, the school teaches Japanese as a foreign language to all students regardless of race or religion.

The school provides students the opportunity to experience Japanese culture as they learn the language. Our program provides a rich variety of cultural activities including monthly cultural events to enhance cultural experience and understanding. It is hoped that the experience at the Southeast Japanese School will provide students with a better understanding of the Japanese people.

We believe that foreign language is best taught at a young age when children are most responsive to new languages. The school includes a kindergarten program for children who are 5 years old. Our regular program is recommended for children 6 years and older. Our program includes all modalities of the language including listening, speaking, reading, writing, and culture.
The school year begins in late August and ends at the end of June.
history.mission: “We, at Southeast Japanese School, are committed to providing instructions in the Japanese language and culture. Our goal is to enable students to successfully function in a Japanese-speaking environment and to foster an appreciation of the Japanese culture.”
